source.title: Anderson Acceleration for Distributed Training of Deep Learning Models
source.authors: Massimiliano Lupo Pasini; Jun-Qi Yin; Viktor Reshniak; M. Stoyanov

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; figure values are not transcribed in the text.
record.tranche_reason: Applies an adaptive moving-average method to ResNet50 training on CIFAR100 and ImageNet1k with large-scale distributed data parallelism, reporting validation-accuracy outcomes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation-accuracy curves and textual descriptions of how AADL and moving average affect the generalization gap. It does not compare large and small batches, so its results do not test V5's batch-size penalty claim directly.
record.test_reason: The study assumes the large-batch generalization gap and evaluates its own AADL and moving-average procedure at one batch size per dataset. It provides no smaller-batch comparison under matched epoch budgets, so it does not test V5. Its optimizer comparisons do not test V4's adaptive-method versus SGD claim, and no other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the conclusion that moving average helps AA recover from the generalization gap during distributed training. The results sections qualify this as partial recovery on both datasets. Escape from steep local minima is the authors' interpretation; the reported experiments do not measure sharpness or directly demonstrate escape.
record.recipe_differences: Uses alternating Anderson acceleration combined with an adaptive moving-average procedure and safeguarding; the study does not reproduce the original large-batch versus small-batch comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported recovery differs by training method: AADL alone does not recover the gap, while AADL with moving average partially recovers it on both datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: On both datasets, the authors report that AADL alone fails to recover from the presumed generalization gap, while AADL with moving average partially recovers. Training times for Nesterov, AADL, and AADL with moving average are respectively 7, 79, and 84 minutes on CIFAR100 and 12, 131, and 135 minutes on ImageNet1k.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested distributed ResNet50 training settings, adding moving average to AADL improves reported validation performance, with substantially greater wall-clock cost than unaccelerated Nesterov.

record.problems: The validation-accuracy values are presented in figures without numerical values in the supplied text. The paper does not provide a small-batch comparison, and it states that hyperparameter configuration was fixed using general guidelines rather than tuned for this analysis.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width-dependent test error beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD, including tuning-dependent differences.
Large-versus-small-batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets, and whether recipe changes reduce that measured penalty.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps or ranking against other measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels are warranted. The method's adaptive moving-average criterion does not make this an adaptive-optimizer comparison of the kind specified by V4. All row states are cannot_determine relative to the claim versions; the authors' qualitative method-comparison findings remain recorded under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison with natural-label generalization.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold comparison.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.

The study uses large global batches but does not compare them with smaller batches under a fixed epoch budget. It tests AADL and moving-average effects on the reported generalization gap, not the version's batch-size comparison.
No sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.
